entry.title: The Best Coupe Glasses, According to Bartenders
entry.summary: A delicate, elegant vessel that will elevate everything from cava to Diet Coke.
entry.content:
Nothing in the world makes me feel fancier than a coupe. Stemmed and with a wide, shallow bowl, the dainty glasses enhance the loveliness of a cocktail or a splash of sparkling wine (they’re also referred to as “Champagne saucers”). As a longtime home bartender and food-and-drinks writer, I regularly gravitate toward the coupe for martinis, sparkling wines, nonalcoholic aperitifs, and even Diet Coke. From “coupettes” to engraved statement pieces, there is surprising diversity among coupe glasses, which vary in stem length (typically between 3.5 and 4.5 inches) and bowl diameter (2.5 to 3.5 inches), glass thickness, and color.

Because coupe glasses can dress up such a wide variety of drinks, they make a smart glass choice for stocking your home bar. Lydia Friar, bar manager at Stones Throw in York, Maine, recommends hitting your local thrift store or antiques boutique to start your coupe collection — “when you hold it, you [will] know.” When she got married, she collected more than 150 vintage coupes to serve guests. She looks for “a thin glass, medium length stem, and color when selecting my own vessel. You don’t need all that intricate etching to make a coupe fancy. Sometimes it’s the bold curves of a coupe that make it special.”

In addition to antique finds, there is also a wide variety of stylish, professional-quality coupes you can purchase new for your home bar. I spoke with bartenders, cocktail experts, and sommeliers about the coupe glasses they love to use and what they like to serve in them. If you’re looking for other essential barware, check out our guides to cocktail strainers and jiggers.

Updated on November 3, 2026
These coupes have been updated with the latest pricing and availability.

With a bowl that holds 10.25 ounces, these thin but sturdy glasses are on the larger side for a coupe, but that’s why Bernadette James, certified sommelier at Stages at One Washington and The Living Room in Dover, New Hampshire, loves them so much. “There’s more room for a voluminous drink, from say, an egg or egg white,” she says. “A large glass is also nice for a normal martini because there isn’t the danger of spilling a drink where liquid is all the way to the rim.” They’re pretty but durable. “They are thin enough to feel delicate but sturdy enough not to break during normal use.”

There’s no more glamorous place to drink from a coupe glass than the Ritz Bar in Paris, and head bartender Romain de Courcy loves these elegant, sculptural coupes from Nude, which have slightly weighted bottoms. “I would use those for any short drink served up from a martini or a Manhattan to a daiquiri or an Aviation,” he says. “Just make sure to put them in the freezer for at least ten minutes before use so they keep the cocktail chilled when you pour it in.” Zeynep Özgüvenç, head bartender at Conrad Istanbul Bosphorus, likes Nude coupes in part because they’re designed by renowned bartender Rémy Savage and “exemplify his modern and minimalist aesthetic.”

At Bobby Nashville, head bartender and general manager Jodi Zuber likes retro-feeling coupes with lots of character, and these fun, stumpy little ones fit the bill. “I love the charm of vintage glassware collected from thrift stores, with each piece telling its own story,” says Zuber. “For those seeking that nostalgic feel on a thrift store budget, Godinger offers vintage-inspired, lead-free designs that are extremely durable.” The brand’s Champagne coupe is dishwasher-safe and quite sturdy. Zuber’s favorite cocktail to drink out of it is a Bourbon sour.

For a more slender, daintier coupe, these coupetini glasses from Nude are a bartender favorite. “A great coupe glass, in my opinion, is versatile and not too thick or bulky,” says Zana Möhlmann, bartender at Manhattan Bar in Conrad Singapore Orchard. “The ‘coupetini’ is a perfect example — it can elegantly hold a shaken daisy cocktail as well as a stirred down, spirit-forward drink like a martini or Manhattan.” Möhlmann feels that the thin rim of these glasses enhances the drinking experience. Cody Pruitt, owner of the French bistro Libertine in New York City, is also a fan of these coupetinis because they blend “the classic archetypal V-shaped martini glass and a softer coupe style,” he says. “I don’t love overly rounded, thick-lipped coupes, and I also try to avoid the top-heavy ones that are more appropriate for serving dessert than cocktails. It’s beautiful on the table, lovely to drink out of, and looks much more precious than it actually is.”

Not all coupes are meant to be sleek, and these textured, gold-rimmed coupes are a playful vessel for cocktails. At The Davenport Lounge, located inside the Ritz-Carlton, New Orleans, bartender Brittany DeBlois loves to use vintage-inspired coupes for both Champagne and cocktails, and she serves Paper Planes in these cute Art Deco-style glasses “because the orange color of the drink looks fantastic in a gold-rimmed glass.”

Daniel Padberg, director of food and beverage at The Americano in Atlanta, loves these delicate, lightweight coupe glasses for their “elegance and simplicity.” Holding 8.47 fluid ounces, the sleek crystal coupes “work great for classics, like a vesper and gin martini,” says Padberg, and make a sophisticated vessel for Champagne.

Some coupe glasses evoke chalices, and these ornately patterned options are maximalist fun. At Brassica, located inside the Waldorf Astoria Atlanta Buckhead, Cara McInerney uses many glasses from the Bormioli Rocco 1920s line — including the fizz and sour glasses — but loves these coupes for martinis and mimosas. “The coupe has a lovely scalloping that just shines in our moody, inviting lighting,” she says. With a cool Art Deco look and extra thin rims, these coupes lend themselves perfectly to the ever-popular espresso martini.

These sparkling, dazzling crystal glasses have a chic angular design. At Winona’s in Brooklyn, owner Cressida Greening uses a number of glasses from Zwiesel, but loves this coupe glass the best because “it is the perfect blend of elegance and durability and makes our cocktails look and taste amazing,” she says. Greening serves the restaurant’s Passion Sour, a take on the pisco sour, out of the glass. “We use Chinola Passion Fruit Liqueur for an exotic twist and this glass is the perfect vessel for those aromas to sing,” she says.

Home bartenders should prioritize glassware that is dishwasher-safe and break-resistant. Little Dipper beverage director Alyssa Sartor loves these distinctively etched coupe glasses because they are both of those things, all while still having “the classic, clean look that you’d find in any professional bar setting,” she says. “My go-to drink to serve in this type of glass would be any version of a sour.” The entire Crafthouse by Fortessa barware line is designed by World Champion bartender Charles Joly.

entry.title: Give Them 150-Year-Old Soap
entry.summary: From the smell to the ingredients and lathering factor, it’s an especially satisfying gift.
entry.content:
Bar soap has a rich, alluring history — the earliest recorded recipe was found on a tablet in ancient Babylon, dating from 2200 BC, which consisted of three basic ingredients: water, an alkali (also called lye), and oil of Cassia. From there, it spread to ancient Rome and across Europe, though bathing wasn’t as popular in the U.K. until soap-makers emerged in the 12th century. With the advent of the railroad, the heavily taxed item became a full-fledged industry by the 19th century.

Since then, bar soap has not only become an essential everyday item — it’s also had a bit of a renaissance lately. Loewe, Soft Services, Topicals, and Glossier have all launched bar soaps recently, and some people are taking to eBay to buy bar soaps that are no longer in production. But you don’t have to bid on old soaps on eBay to get ones from brands that have been around for centuries. Plenty of very old companies, like Santa Maria Novella and Roger & Gallet, are still making their classic formulas — and they happen to make great gifts, too. Sure, a nice body gel is practical, but there’s just something more appealing and gratifying about giving a bar of soap with a decades-old story behind it.

And so may I suggest: Give them a 150-year-old bar of soap this holiday season. From the smell to the ingredients and lathering factor, it’s an especially satisfying gift. Here, I’ve rounded up some of the best ones out there, many of which have been around for over a century (at least).

Updated on November 3, 2026
All the soaps recommended below have been updated with the latest pricing and availability.

Reportedly found throughout illustrious homes across Europe since the 19th century — Catherine de’ Medici’s gave its oldest scent as a wedding gift to her future husband, Henry II of Valois — the Santa Maria Novella brand refers to its solid soaps as “small pieces of extraordinary craftsmanship.” It’s not wrong — the soaps themselves are beautifully shaped with the scent name carved elegantly onto the bar, and they work well for sensitive skin. Offering 25 different types of soap, the Florentine soap-maker is known for making bars that are long lasting both in the shower and out — you might even consider leaving a bar of its Melograno soap in your lingerie drawer to keep underwear smelling fresh.

Originating in Porto, Portugal, the soap brand Claus Porto has been in business since 1887. It offers 30 different soaps, which you can get in curated box sets with soaps that have scents inspired by the Portuguese landscape. Each soap is made with natural oils that create a luxe-feeling lather, and some soaps come on ropes (pictured above), which make them easier to hold or hang up after using. They make especially eye-catching gifts — like this three-piece set with a soap dish — thanks to their colorful, eclectic wrapping. 

Genoese soap-maker Valobra has been around since 1903 and blends a combination of three simple ingredients — soda, coconut oil, and tallow — using an ancient technique called “levata da lisciva” to ensure that the soap is free from impurities. To make the “finest” soap in the world, it is then matured for two months before it’s sold to customers. The ergonomic shape is “intentionally designed to nestle seamlessly in the palm of the hand, allowing for a pleasant grip that releases a fragrant, dense lather,” according to C.O. Bigelow, the West Village apothecary that was founded in 1838, where you can find Valobra soaps.

Since 1840, Klar Seifen has been producing vegan soap by using a mix of modern manufacturing techniques plus handmade craftsmanship using molds that are nearly 100 years old. The brand’s thick and dense soaps come wrapped in beautiful floral paper, and are also available in the form of shampoo and conditioner bars. They even have this clove-scented Christmas special that would make a particularly festive gift.

According to Roger & Gallet, a brand that launched its first soap in 1879, this soap is made in a cauldron (!). This one in particular has a candied-ginger scent with notes of berries and pomegranate. Overall, it’s warm and sensual — and it comes in a gorgeous little box. You can find this one at C.O. Bigelow, too.

Caswell-Massey has been around since before the founding of the United States. Its plant-based, triple-milled soaps produce an “ultrarich” lather and come in old-timey (but very nice!) scents like lavender and sandalwood. The soaps are sold individually and as sets. According to the brand, Caswell-Massey’s signature scent, Number Six, is the longest continuously manufactured American fragrance.

Cella Milano has been selling its cream beard soap since 1899 — and, in fact, was awarded the gold medal at the International Exhibition of Milan in 1906 and the Grand Cross of Industrial Merit in 1908. Its “surprisingly gentle” beard soap has a lovely almond scent and can be lathered up to create a creamy, soft, firm foam that helps a blade glide over the skin to ensure an irritation-free shave and fresh skin.

[Editor’s Note: If you prefer to give this cream soap in bar form, Cella offers a refill bar for the container above.]

Established in 1760, Creed offers hand-milled soaps infused with the brand’s best-selling fragrances, including Aventus and Green Irish Tweed. Creed actually has several royal connections — in an 1860 article in the Army and Navy Gazette, it was noted that James Henry Creed, the founder of the brand, was awarded a special appointment to Queen Victoria and principal courts in Europe. Plus, he also worked in D’Antin in Paris, for the tailors Messrs Harris & Co., which is where he would have created garments for European royalty. Additionally, Creed created a riding habit for Queen Victoria in 1885 that can be found in the Kyoto Museum, which inspired the brand’s campaign for its best-selling female fragrance, Aventus for Her. All of that is to say: Give this very old soap to the Anglophile on your list.

entry.title: These Are the Best Roasting Pans for Your Thanksgiving Turkey
entry.summary: Multipurpose vessels for year-round cooking — and the once-a-year big bird.
entry.content:
Turkey is the cornerstone of the Thanksgiving table. Yet it has a mid reputation, mostly because it can be difficult to cook well. It is a big bird, which means it’s harder to nail the exact right time and temperature to make every bite perfect than it is with, say, a chicken. Some people swear by a wet brine, others dry. Some stuff it; others don’t. Some stick the whole thing in the oven, and others break it down by parts before cooking.

But no matter what, the cookware you use is part of the equation. I’ll start by telling you about my favorite option — a piece of equipment I think is worth investing in for this task and beyond. Misen’s roasting pan is somewhat of a combination of a roasting pan and a sheet pan. It’s significantly less bulky than the traditional form. Still, it has higher sides than a standard sheet pan, which means it can hold big, juicy pieces of meat, and it features substantial handles on each side so you can comfortably lift it.

Like a traditional roasting pan, the Misen version is made from stainless steel. “It cleans up so easily and always looks new after,” Strategist senior editor Winnie Yang says of the material; she pulls hers out multiple times a week. “I know some people like the patina you get on aluminum sheet pans, but they also get kind of a sticky residue sometimes, and that never happens with the Misen.”

It comes in nine-inch and 13-inch sizes, but the largest 18-inch pan (just big enough that I nestle my half-sheets right inside for storage) is what works best for large cuts. This past Thanksgiving, it held my butchered turkey in the fridge as the bird dry-brined for two days. It caught leaking juices and felt not at all precarious to lift out and clean up. I then cooked the turkey directly on it with great success. From there, it was easy to scrape up and pour out all the browned bits for gravy. (Indeed, you can technically do this directly in the roasting pan on top of the stove, though I prefer to transfer the bits into a saucepan so whisking is easy.)

Of course, you could use it for roasted potatoes, carrots, or Brussels sprouts — as well as any number of foods throughout the year. It happens to be especially great for turkey, but it certainly isn’t a one-and-done situation. Still, if this doesn’t appeal, there are other options.

A traditional roasting pan with even higher sides gets the job done too. The biggest downside is storage, but if you have the space, that’s not an issue. In that case, All-Clad’s stainless-steel version is a great bet. The brand makes some of the best skillets and saucepans on the market in that material, and this pan is no different. All-Clad offers an especially large model with a stainless-steel insert, which I think is unnecessarily bulky. This one, though, looks just a bit heftier than the Misen.

On the other end of the spectrum, a regular half-sheet pan works well, too — a method I learned from Alison Roman. You start with a wire rack fitted inside one pan for the brining process so juices can drip down without making the bottom of the bird gross. Then you transfer the turkey to a clean tray to cook. It’s a little more precarious to maneuver it in and out of the oven than with the Misen or All-Clad but certainly not impossible. Cooking-wise, it works well, as sheet pans emit very even heat. (Roman also notes if you cook vegetables to the side of the bird, they get really nicely browned.) You also probably already have one — and if you don’t, they’re much cheaper than roasting pans. And of course, they can be used for many other purposes throughout the year.

If you are not big into cooking or have a super-small kitchen but have been tasked with the turkey this year, buying a disposable pan for such a specific task isn’t a bad move. It is really cheap and can be done away with after the holiday. The biggest downside here is that it’s much thinner overall, which means heat conduction won’t be as good as any of the options above — but it can get the job done if you prefer to prioritize convenience.

entry.title: Italy With 11 Kids Under 10? How to Plan an Extreme Family Trip
entry.summary: Make it the best (or at least most memorable) vacation you ever take.
entry.content:
A gigantic family vacation with three sets of cousins and grandparents along for the ride is no time to wing it Anthony Bourdain style. Strategic packing and a flexible yet well-considered itinerary are key to making big multigenerational trips work, both on the road and once you make it to your destination.

To help you plan (and when you’re planning for this many people, it’s certainly best to start doing so well in advance) I asked 20 parents with extensive experience traveling with lots of kids and other relatives for their best tips. Whether you’re road-tripping to a lake house, spending a week at a Disney resort, or trekking to Machu Picchu with ten 2-year-olds, here’s how to make sure an extended family trip is the best — or at least the most memorable — you ever undertake.

Travel agent and Adventures of a Disney Dad founder Matt Brandabur, who vacations with five kids aged 8 and under, says remaining hands-free is critical: “The baby carrier we love is the BabyBjörn Baby Carrier Free. Since we had twins, it was even more useful because both parents can carry a baby while also having free hands to help with the other kids.”

He adds that double strollers are a game changer and recommends a collapsible model like the UPPAbaby G-Link V2 Double Umbrella Stroller (which, unfortunately, is sold out everywhere): “It’s great quality, and the lightweight size makes it easier to carry through the airport when also carrying luggage, other kids, or car seats.” Magic Expeditions travel agent Alison Assner recommends the City Mini GT2 (which also collapses quickly and folds one-handed) as an alternative, and the Strategist’s resident stroller expert, Liza Corsillo, directed me to Zoe’s lightweight and compact Twin V3. For more adventurous trips, Brandabur tries to rent a double BOB Gear jogging stroller (“it has shocks and is easier to maneuver on uneven surfaces”) once he gets to his destination.

As for car rides, for kids aged 4 and older, Essner likes to bring along the BubbleBum inflatable booster seat. “It collapses flat for packing, but you can quickly blow it up if you need to hop in an Uber or taxi.”

Clearsurance travel-insurance expert Melanie Musson and her sister take their families on a joint summer vacation every year, and they always add several day hikes to the itinerary to keep everyone busy. Eight of their combined 11 kids are currently under the age of 10, so this seems ambitious. “But we have the best time,” she promises. Good gear is key, and she recommends the Kinderpack baby carrier, which remains “so comfortable, even on long hikes.”

She also likes to give each child a CamelBak Mini Mule water-bladder backpack. “They get to pack snacks and one or two small toys of their choice,” she explains. “Then they have what they need to keep themselves happy, but the adults aren’t stuck carrying it.”

“If my kids have naps or quiet time at home, I try my best to keep a similar schedule on vacation,” says Brandabur. If you’re entering different time zones with a big group of kids, there are ways to signal when it’s time to get some shut-eye, says travel agent LaDell Carter, who took 12 members of her family to Italy and Switzerland this past summer: “With younger children, I put them in their pajamas before we even leave for the airport — I want them boarding the aircraft already understanding that this is bedtime.” And when boarding a flight, “never check the lovie, blanket, or pacifier because those keep naps happening in an unfamiliar place,” says Essner. One exception: You might consider relaxing family screen-time rules on travel days. “A favorite movie can buy you an entire flight.”

If your flight gets in early and you have the budget for it, Carter suggests booking your hotel room for the night prior to arrival so you don’t have to wait around for a 2 p.m. check-in. “Otherwise, you may have an exhausted toddler still wearing pajamas, tired grandparents, teenagers who want Wi-Fi and a shower, and hours to fill,” Carter says.

“Duffels over suitcases,” recommends Foley PR co-founder Jen Boersma, who travels with her six kids. “Hard suitcases are wonderful right up until you are stacking eight of them in a minivan. Duffels squash, stack, and slide into the gaps. The only hard case we bring is the one that holds anything breakable.”

Viktor Marohnić, founder and CEO of 57hours, essentially only takes his family on extreme trips in terms of destinations — his youngest daughter spent a week camping in Yosemite when she was just 4 weeks old. So he only invests in the most durable, family-friendly adventure gear, such as Patagonia’s Black Hole duffel, which comes with backpack straps. It “survives being thrown into a van, a boat, or onto a mule, or anywhere a roller bag doesn’t,” he says.

If you just can’t do without roller bags or are contending with mobility issues, duffels with wheels offer “the perfect mix of space, usability, and utility,” says the Luminaire founder Adam Sebba.

Strategist senior editor Jen Trolio went on an 11-person (including five kids ages 3 to 10) family trip to Disney World Orlando last year that required packing skills of steel. A big takeaway was that non-clamshell suitcases take up a lot less valuable hotel-room space when everyone’s competing for it. She likes Away’s flexible Softside Carry-on, which has one deep packing compartment rather than two and can be rummaged around in with ease.

Whichever luggage you use, try to reduce its size and choose accommodations with laundry facilities instead of bringing lots of spare clean clothing. “For these trips, if everybody has massive suitcases, then it really limits what you can do, and makes every transfer a pain,” says Richard Campbell, founder of 10Adventures.

On the subject of luggage, “one thing I have learned about traveling with children is that they love feeling involved,” says Carter. “They want to help pack. They want to carry something. They want to feel as though they have an important role in the adventure.” So let them have their own (appropriately sized) bag, especially as it means you won’t have to carry it yourself once they’re past a certain age.

Boersma also says “one bag per child” is the way to go. “The moment you start packing by category instead of by person, you own every outfit decision for the entire trip. If it is their bag, they know what is in it, and a 9-year-old can get themselves dressed.”

It’s still a good idea to bring one additional family “float” bag where the shared stuff lives, says CityMoms founder Jeanine Bobenmoyer: “Extra chargers, a mini-first-aid kit, sunscreen, the stuff that’s shared between everyone.” Her other nonnegotiable is a dedicated dirty-laundry bag. “Book an Airbnb with laundry or schedule a laundromat stop near the end of the trip — coming home with clean clothes is a gift to your future self.”

Mom of eight Linda Perillo, whose mom runs Perillo Tours, has eight kids and a lifetime of travel experience. She says that doing a dollar-store run before the trip and letting everybody pack their own snack bag “eliminates the ‘Mom, do you have’ routine and gives them some sense of control while giving me some peace.”

Ziplocs work great as snack bags, and Carter also recommends Stasher’s silicone bags, which she’ll often fill up at the hotel breakfast buffet with fruit for later: “They are reusable, easy to rinse, and useful for everything from snacks to small travel accessories.”

Keeping one parent in charge of all the travel documents “helps reduce airport chaos,” says Sebba. The risk of one family member leaving their passport in their plane seat pocket just isn’t worth taking.

When it comes to kids’ toys, alongside everyone’s favorite stuffed animals, “I always save a few surprises specifically for travel,” says Carter. “Something they have not played with every day at home tends to hold their attention a little longer.” She likes suction toys for young children who might need to be entertained while waiting in lines and at airport lounges and also recommends packs of temporary tattoos to mark the trip. “My biggest rule is to avoid games with dozens of tiny pieces,” she adds. “There is nothing enjoyable about crawling underneath an airplane seat searching for a miniature game piece while the person behind you is trying to sleep.”

“If you’re traveling with eight or more people, I wouldn’t plan every activity for everyone together,” says Andrés Serra, head of operations at Optimise Travel. “I suggest having one group activity in the morning, giving two options in the afternoon, and meeting up for dinner. Before splitting up, make sure everyone knows when and where to meet, how they’ll get around, and which adults will be with each group.”

Aim for one big group event or meal per day — and because restaurant reservations for groups of ten people can be tricky to get, book well ahead of time or cook together at your accommodation.

On road trips with big groups, “having multiple cars is easier,” says family-travel expert Emilie Brillon, who recently road-tripped to San Diego with two families. “We rented a seven-person car and all traveled together, but it would have been nice to have two cars so my sister could have gone back to the house to put the little baby down for a nap when it was getting to be too much.”

Compass realtor Stephanie Moon recently spent a ten-day Alaskan cruise with 39 extended family members and friends. While it was important for everybody to have their own space and downtime, card games united the group when needed. “Piles! was the biggest hit for this year,” she says. “At first, it was my nuclear family playing, then the cousins, and one night, all the kids, young adults, and aunties.” Similarly, “some of our funniest family travel memories happen when everyone gathers in one room to play a card game,” says Carter. “We recently returned from Lancaster, Pennsylvania, and everyone was playing Taco Cat Goat Cheese Pizza until midnight.”

When traveling with a large group that includes a bunch of teenagers, Serra recommends putting “more of the budget toward good accommodation and less toward booking lots of paid activities” because teens prefer to choose how to spend their time and are less inclined to stick to regimented schedules. A centrally located hotel within walking distance of local attractions is ideal for these scenarios.

He suggests giving each teen “a small cross-body bag for their room card, portable charger, and emergency contacts” before letting them roam free. “Also,” he says, “save an offline copy of the itinerary on everyone’s phone with two meeting spots and a contact number in case someone can’t get online.”

“My big kids help with the little ones,” says Fun Park Go travel agent Alan Eskelsen, who’s a single dad of six. “When you’re the only parent, you need a team. I pair each older kid with a younger one for the day. The younger one has a buddy, and the older one feels trusted.” For park trips, he also suggests getting everybody the same brightly colored T-shirt so they can be spotted from a distance.

“Because keeping track of 12 people is enough,” Carter advises putting AirTags (or similar Android-compatible Bluetooth trackers, such as Tiles or Samsung SmartTags) in “checked luggage, carry-ons, backpacks, and sometimes smaller bags that have a habit of being left behind.” (Apple’s FindMy app allows you to label AirTags and other trackers so you know which items they are tracking.) She adds that if lots of people are using the same brand of suitcase or duffel, it’s worth purchasing custom luggage tags for each person to visually differentiate the bags at a glance. For similar reasons, “I recommend getting packing cubes in different colors for each family member,” says Voyagers Travel Company adviser Maria Emilia.

While not as plush as regular cotton towels, microfiber alternatives are essential when you’re heading to the beach for the day with 11 kids, says Musson. “They’re much easier for parents to carry in a beach bag.” They’re also easier to wash in the hotel sink or beach shower and will dry much more quickly.

You’ll definitely want to chronicle your big family trip, but who takes the multigenerational group photo? “One of our best travel purchases is a collapsible phone tripod,” says Sund. “We set a ten-second timer and get photos with the whole family, even somewhere remote where nobody is around to help.”

Marohnić always hires a local guide on his family trips, even if he understands the destination well. This way, he says, you’ve got one person who knows the area, makes the safety calls, and (“this is the part parents underrate”) can be the voice of authority. “Kids will listen to a guide when they’ve long stopped listening to their parents,” he says. Guides are also pretty good at taking group shots if you forgot to take along a tripod.

For kids who are digitally detoxing and need to be kept busy, Whitt likes bringing offline games and art supplies. She also recommends packing a pair of compact, kid-size binoculars, plus an old-fashioned compass that they can learn how to use on the trip.

“Give each kid a project: a disposable or camp camera to shoot on the trip or a scavenger hunt you set up the first morning,” says Elena Rodriguez, founder of Studio Roam Travel. “It gives them something to do that isn’t asking you what’s next.” Instant cameras are also a hit, says Julie Day of multigenerational travel agency Gatherwell Travel. “Kids can use it themselves — some of our favorite photos from family vacations were taken by our kids on a Fuji Instax Mini.”

Everyone I spoke with advised forming travel plans around the youngest or slowest member of your family group. Still, you should also trust they can do more than you think. “We always treated our kids like they were capable, and when you go in with that mind-set, it surprises you how much more they can do,” says Marohnić.

There are lots of adventurous destinations that hold up for big groups of mixed ages, says GearJunkie founder Stephen Regenold, who has five kids. Hut-to-hut hiking in the Dolomites or the Alps is a wonderful option because you can eat at restaurants on the trail and “there’s enough infrastructure that you’re not lugging too much gear.” (To avoid the Instagram crowds, he says Slovenia’s Julian Alps are “the quieter, cheaper version of the Dolomites.”) He also recommends Iceland for an outdoorsy group trip because it’s a place where “everyone is outside and you’ll see grandparents and toddlers on the same trail.”

Host of the Family Travel Unpacked podcast Melissa Conn plans a wintertime family trip with over a dozen family members each year, including seven kids ranging from 5 to 20 years old. And while they’ve experimented with all types of trips, the easiest “has definitely been a cruise,” she says. That’s because there’s always something going on for everyone, from sports to karaoke to pool time. And “the all you can eat at all hours is perfect for teens’ weird sleep schedules and hollow legs,” she adds.

Choose a cruise line with an onboard nursery for babies and toddlers if you’ve got young kids with you (“Disney Cruise Line and Royal Caribbean are good choices,” says Essner), so the adults get to enjoy at least one grown-up dinner. If you’ve got teenagers, consider a smaller expedition-style cruise. “The Galápagos Islands are perfect for this because the destination does much of the entertaining for you,” says Emilia. “Instead of parents constantly having to convince people to put their phones down, the days are filled with snorkeling alongside sea lions, kayaking, spotting giant tortoises, and discovering extraordinary wildlife.”

For trips on dry land, Disney resorts work well, although not all Disney accommodations are made equal. “We love the family suites at Disney’s Art of Animation Resort,” says Eskelsen. “You get a separate bedroom, a pull-out couch, and a table that folds down into a bed. The best part is the two full bathrooms. There’s also a mini-fridge and microwave, so we do breakfast in the room and save a lot of money.”

entry.title: Ask a Picky Guy: Stain-Hiding Duds for Dads
entry.summary: Plus Patagonia alternatives, a fall shoe report, and a Viberg boot review.
entry.content:
Whether he’s overhauling the Menswear Hall of Fame, trying on every sweater at J.Crew, or profiling the Zoomer tailor of the moment for New York’s inaugural “Men’s Style” issue, senior writer Michael Zhao has quickly become the Strategist’s resident picky guy. He’s here to answer your questions about men’s style, highly specific appliance hunts, impossible gifting assignments, and whatever else you need a picky guy’s take on. Send your questions to pickyguy@nymag.com.

As a new father myself who’s already running into this issue, I have limited experience to offer and, frankly, could use advice as well. So I polled some of the most stylish dads I know for their sage counsel.

“I think you need to embrace the reality that no matter what you wear, your toddler will find a way to visibly stain it,” said Michael B. Dougherty of Mensweird. “That being said, I find lighter neutrals hide snot and grease better than dark colors. Or just wear camo and let people guess if the pattern is flecktarn or Go-Gurt.”

Chris Gentile, the owner and head designer of Pilgrim Surf + Supply, recommended dark earth tones for everything except spit-up milk — which might be fine for a 2-year-old. But he added that patterns are more effective than any specific color in hiding stains: “Mid-tone check, plaid, stripes, and patterns are by far the best at hiding stains. Think houndstooth chef pants.”

“Navy served me well before, during, and after the toddler phase,” said restaurateur and shirting designer Brooks Reitz. “But that’s probably just because that’s what I’ve always loved.” Founder and designer of 18 East Antonio Ciongoli also recommended staying the course: “White and own it. I never switched up my fits at all with three kids.”

I’ll add that wool fabrics resist stains exceptionally well because the residual lanolin that coats the fibers prevents liquids from soaking in. (We’ve been loving our new CB2 rug for this reason.) Pendleton flannels (plentiful and affordable on eBay) are a classic, but there are thinner, less hot wool fabrics as well.

Patagonia boyfriend is definitely a type — and one that’s hard to grow out of, for good reason. The brand’s decadeslong commitment to high-quality, relatively sustainable materials and durable construction is enough for many to look past its often unflattering cuts. Its clothes may not be the most fashion-forward, but the fact that its pieces pair easily in any combination appeals to guys who see getting dressed as a chore rather than an opportunity for self-expression. Here are a few other brands and lines doing something similar that should integrate easily with his existing wardrobe.

Outerknown was started by pro surfer Kelly Slater, but the quality of its clothes transcends its celebrity-founder origins. It began 11 years ago with the Blanket Shirt, an elevated overshirt take on the surfer-beloved blanket ponchos — colloquially known as “drug rugs.” Since then, its offerings have expanded into every clothing category a boyfriend could ever need, plus a decent women’s line. Like Patagonia, it prioritizes sustainable materials and responsible factories wherever possible.

Gramicci is as deeply enmeshed with climbing culture as Patagonia. It started in the ’80s with the original G-Pant, which combined the gusseted crotch and pull-on design of karate pants with hard-wearing cotton canvas construction to create tough, easy-wearing, crag-ready pants. It’s expanded its line of Japanese-streetwear-inspired tops and jackets in recent years.

Like Arc’teryx’s Veilance, Red Box is the North Face’s more fashion-forward sub-label. However, unlike Veilance, it’s not significantly more expensive than the main brand’s collections. The silhouettes are definitely on the trendier side, so I’m not sure he’ll go for it, but it’s worth considering.

Finally, maybe it’s okay if he sticks with Patagonia. As I noted in September’s testing report, the brand’s latest collections are increasingly fashionable, with more logoless designs offered in more contemporary cuts. It hasn’t spun out a sub-label (and I doubt it ever will), but there are plenty of great options if you know where to look.

Like many men who got their style advice online in the mid-2010s, I was enamored with the idea that a pair of welted boots could be bought once and resoled for life. In practice, the ones I bought for around $300 ($440 in today’s dollars!) looked pretty shabby after a year of regular wear — and not in the patinated style I was hoping for. I have had better success with dress shoes, loafers, and derbies in the years since but had given up on the promise of a buy-it-for-life boot until I visited the new Viberg store in Nolita.

After hearing about my experience with previous boots of this style, the clerk pulled several parts from deconstructed Viberg shoes, along with some from other well-known brands for comparison. Viberg’s leather insoles were over twice as thick as the next thickest. The welt flanges were channeled directly into the leather rather than sewn or glued on — a technique that requires antiquated machinery and custom-milled parts to repair. The uppers are stretched drum-tight over the lasts by hand and stitched down all the way around. This laborious process means the brand can produce no more than 10,000 pairs each year, which is why new drops tend to sell out within weeks of release.

I worried that such a sturdy-feeling boot would have a burdensome break-in period, but it was actually quite comfortable from the first wear (they fit true to size, and Viberg offers different lasts for different foot shapes). After six months and hundreds of miles, and despite my lackadaisical shoe-tree use, the leather is only barely beginning to crease. At $1,380 a pair, they cost more than any boot I’ve come across that isn’t from a luxury fashion house. But unlike similar designs from other brands (many of which aren’t much cheaper), Viberg’s boots could actually last you a lifetime.

My colleague Erin Schwartz recently gave some excellent advice on how to banish the clothes chair from your home once and for all. As much as I’d love to do that, I don’t think I have the fortitude and discipline to make it stick. Instead, I opted to replace the Cesca chair with a busted wicker seat that had been languishing beside my dresser with a piece of furniture that was actually designed to be saddled with clothing: a valet.

The Harrington chair comes from Todd Snyder’s recent collaboration with CB2 and is actually meant for holding clothes. Unlike the tall-back versions commonly found in estate sales, this modern style made from gorgeously sculpted solid hardwood is the same size as a regular dining chair, so it can be called on for dinner parties if needed. It’s perfectly sized for hanging shirts and jackets that aren’t ready for the laundry but don’t need to go back in the closet. I also use it to lay out an outfit when I need to try different shirt-jacket-tie combinations before committing. The downside to this compact, dining-friendly design is that it has no pants hanger, and even if it did, it would be too short. But it’s the right size for most men’s needs most of the time.

entry.title: What Nulastin Founder Leah Garcia Buys at the Drugstore
entry.summary: “When I travel, I pour some into the little bottles of hotel-room lotion. It makes it feel luxurious.”
entry.content:
Here at the Strategist, we love hearing about everyday stuff that actually works. That line of thinking extends to the drugstore beauty products in our medicine cabinets, shower caddies, and makeup bags. In our series “Beauty Aisle,” we talk to folks in the beauty industry — aestheticians, hairstylists, makeup artists, dermatologists, and the like — about the go-to affordable products they keep stocked. For this installment, writer Arielle Avila chatted with Nulastin founder Leah Garcia about the drugstore products she loves.

First of all, let me just say this: I am annoyed with the soft cotton end of the swab these days. When I was younger, Q-tips had the softest, fluffiest swab. I’m telling you, I think they changed it. Now, I’m still completely devoted to the brand Q-tips. Why? Same reason why I buy Kleenex, but I’m annoyed. I’m constantly looking for one, so I keep them everywhere. It’s probably the least glamorous thing in my beauty routine, but I’m never without them. I use them to clean up the lash line. The only thing I don’t use it for is if I get mascara on my eyelids. Instead, use a spoolie brush to take it off, especially if you’ve already done your eyeshadow. I learned that from Jamie Greenberg on one of her Instagrams. It takes it right off.

I try to wear sunscreen every single day, and I’m particularly diligent about putting it above and around my brows. Sunglasses don’t always protect that area, and I’ve seen so many women experience brow thinning as they get older. After going through changes in my own hair and brows, it’s an area I’m very conscious about protecting. This is literally my favorite sunscreen in the world. I love the small tip applicator. Now, that being said, I’m on my way to Croatia Wednesday, and I will pick up that same sunscreen, but with BEMT, which is the ingredient that just got approved here in the United States. The sunscreen formulation there is different from the U.S. Same brand, just next-level good. But if I’m in the States and I don’t get to poach a product from Europe, then I will go right into Target and pick this one up. It’s non-comedogenic. I don’t get any acne. It disappears after I’ve put it on.

My God, it’s dreamy. This was given to me as a gift at a conference, and now I’m a junkie. I will get it anywhere if I can. This is something I picked up from childhood. My mom used to use old-school baby oil and blend it with some generic lotion. It gives you a nice glistening glow. Now, I use this every time I shower. And when I travel, I pour some into the little bottles of hotel-room lotion. Those lotions never seem to moisturize at all. But you add this, and now all of a sudden you’ve got whatever generic lotion from a hotel room mixed with that Saltair. It makes it feel luxurious.

Listen, I normally will pick Native because I like the way it looks on my counter. No question. It’s not because I put it on, I go, “Oh, that’s really great.” As a matter of fact, I don’t think I’ve ever read their ingredient deck. It might have dimethicone in it for all I know, which I’ve been trying to avoid. But I buy it first for what it looks like on my counter, which is not right. So my tip would be, read the directions. If you need to adjust, adjust. But I figured that was better than Vaseline, in terms of body lotion. I am a creature of my past, so it’s either Lubriderm, Eucerin, any of those, but I just want a clean, usually white bottle on my vanity. That’s what I’m after.

Who can win with their heels? It’s like pushing the biggest boulder up a hill. No matter how many times I try to get all that calluses off of it, it’s just fighting back. I think the whole thing is disgusting, so I buy new foot files whenever I can. I don’t want that shit reused. I don’t want to be like, “Oh, where’s that heel scrubber from four years ago?” I just get a new one. They’re not that precious. Mine has one of those notches, so that all your little callus junk stays in there. I can’t let all that dead skin go flying everywhere either.

I used to love Crest. I then got told by somebody at one point to use Sensodyne. My husband and I both couldn’t stand the smell of either. I think when you get older, your sense of smell changes and affects what you can and can’t tolerate. I’ve also tried to go into Whole Foods and get some of their toothpaste. First of all, it’s full of air. It looks like a big toothpaste, but it’s not. Then, you use it, and you have to use a lot of it, because it really doesn’t feel like it does much. The consistency feels overly whipped. I can afford to go try these new things, but I feel very strongly that I don’t get nickeled and dimed like a potato chip bag that has a very small amount. I want to get my money’s worth with things like toothpaste. Finally, we switched to Colgate. It’s not the typical one, but a slightly more expensive, bougier one. This Colgate will last me forever.

I don’t mind sweating, but I do mind smelling. Old Spice is a deodorant but not an antiperspirant, so it doesn’t stop sweating. Years ago I was told it’s best not to use antiperspirants, so I’ve just stuck to that. I’ve been using this because it’s easy. Plus, I can share it with my man.

I’ve never missed a day of flossing in the last 35 years. Listen, I don’t know if it’s environmentally really friendly for all of us to be using these, but they are made from recycled plastic. I love the dual floss string as opposed to just the single string. One string will break, and all of the reviews that you see are accurate. A game-changer is that once you get done with the string side‚ you flip down the end of it, and then the other end is a pick to get up into your gums. It’s a process, but it feels really good. My husband and I affectionately call them harpsichords, even though it’s not even shaped like a harpsichord. I don’t know why, but we say, “Did you pack your harpsichord?”

I don’t wash my hair every day; I wash about every fourth day. On those days I need to throw my hair in a fun bun, I use a scrunchie. I can’t even use an old school ponytail holder anymore. It has to have a soft silk or cotton around it. I’m not particular about the brand, I just like something soft and easy that I can throw my hair up with without fussing over it. I loan them out all the time to my friends, so I’m constantly having to buy new ones.

entry.title: What Erika Alexander Can’t Live Without
entry.summary: “I recently bought Hillary Clinton some stationery from there.”
entry.content:
If you’re like us, you’ve probably wondered what everyday stuff famous people add to their carts — like mascara or a sleep mask. We asked actress and comedian Erika Alexander — who stars in season two of The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins — about the scalp oil, cotton T-shirts, and body butter she can’t live without.

So a lot of people have been talking about bonnets and whether they are appropriate and all of those things. But for many years, people have been wearing scarves. I think there’s a kind of renewed interest in scarves, not just from a cultural point of view, but from a reference of those in the Deco period; they always wore these beautiful scarves. It didn’t matter what color you were or where you were from. And so this is kind of a nod to the beauty of those scarves, but she adds wire to make it sculptural. So when I’m not having my hair in a wig or anything on, how can I look really coiffed? I grab that silk scarf and I wire it up, put some earrings on, and I look like I’m ready to shop or get on a plane.
And the silk, of course, is good for preventing breakage in my hair. I love it. Ashaka Givens also used to be Erykah Badu’s hatter.

The Gymwrap is by my friend Nicole Ari Parker. Again, there’s emphasis on my hair and laying these edges down, but also making sure so they don’t break. Having edges at this age especially is a result of wrapping my hair up at night. But when you sweat and you go to the gym, you need something to not only catch the sweat but to keep the hair from getting wet. It will start to draw down. But it doesn’t do that with this. And it’s successful for Nicole. She’s an actress like me. I really love that she’s an entrepreneur. It actually works.
I don’t just put it on when I’m walking or working out. I put it on the shower to protect from the mist and humidity. I’ll also wear it to travel, and I’ll wear it with Akash’s scarf on so I don’t get any of the oil and stuff on my scarf. I’ll put it on as an in-between thing.

I went into Pineider’s Rockefeller Center boutique after noticing it had beautiful leathers. I bought quite a few bags, and one of them was this shoulder bag in a beautiful orange, which I like. I’m really trying to be conscious now and not just buy a bag because it’s expensive or has a logo.

And it turns out that they not only do bags, but they do pens and stationery too, and I love to write. My favorite pen is a beautiful ballpoint pen that has enamel on it and gold tongue. I now buy all my stationery and gifts from there. I recently bought Hillary Clinton some stationery from there, which I have to send to her because it was just her birthday. She’s one of my mentors in life. And of course, she would appreciate it because I’ve gotten so many thank you letters from her that were written by her and signed by her. I think she’s old school in a way that she understands that people don’t often send correspondence that way, but one of the most precious things I have is my stack of letters from her.

[While Erika didn’t specify which stationery item from Pineider she likes the most, we’ve linked to a similar item on its site here.]

I met the co-founder Stephen Satterfield while he was hosting the Netflix series High on the Hog. After that gig he went into sourcing cotton after hearing about Black farmers who didn’t know how to distribute their cotton. So he created Comoco T-shirts so they could have a place to put their cotton. It’s fantastic. They have both a white and black T-shirt. I love it, and think people should know about it, because it’s actually beautiful cotton. It’s made here in America, and you’re supporting farmers and Black people in the South.

I get the small, but I think that you should order a little bigger because I don’t think it’s preshrunk.

About five or six years ago, I was at Brooklyn Bowl and learned about this body butter from the Black women working at the shoe rental counter. She had a bottle of Don’t Be Ashy next to her on the counter, which turned out to be her side business. I bought a couple, because I like to buy things to give when I visit people on Broadway, whether it’s Audra McDonald, Joy Reid, or Nikole Hannah Jones. I’ve now given several people Don’t Be Ashy. You can’t beat this body butter. It’s the best.

My makeup artist, Frederick Sanders, uses a bunch of different things, but I find that on me, this deep red, Bawse Lady, just happens to be a really pretty red, especially on my skin, which has a lot of red in it. This has a little blue in it. It’s really nice and deep and sexy and bright. I also like the name of it.

I discovered this at one of my favorite shops, Layla, in Brooklyn. The perfume itself is from a Los Angeles perfumer, Leanne Hirsh, who makes natural colognes with natural ingredients. Beautiful, unique smells. Choita is what sent me to her. It’s really nice, not sweet or musky. It’s got a good balance. It smells like you’re in an inn, somewhere in New Hampshire or someplace that’s kind of old and worn, but bright, because it’s got a woodiness. But I like sweet smells, so I can smell that there too.

She also gives perfume-making classes. So I took a class with her, and now I’ve made my own perfume called Maverick. I then just went down the rabbit hole with her. She’s fantastic, and I just love everything she does, but this is my favorite perfume from her.

I buy people these robes when I don’t know what to give them. These are also from my favorite shop Layla’s. When my boyfriend was losing his mother, his two aunties were there and were always sitting on the couch in their clothes. So I said, “I’m gonna get them these robes.” And they lived in those robes while she passed away. They’re hand-blocked, cotton, and prewashed. They turned out to be perfect for them, and they still love them. I have one too, but I love to give them as well.

This is a dress you could put on a president or an empress. It’s just beautiful and I love the way it hinges at the hips. It’s a dress that you can wear anywhere. I like to wear it for press and speaking engagements. This color is a good color; it’s not a hard red, it’s kind of a saffron red. I also just love the way Sergio makes clothes. I love his story. I like the way he came into fashion and built something for himself, and all the word of mouth on him meets the moment. He’s a good man who knows how to make clothes.

I spend a lot of time dealing with my hair. On my current set I have Nray Locs, so I have to oil my scalp a lot, but it can’t look too oily. This oil is perfect. My hairdresser for The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins, Roseline Davies, who’s Liberian American, created it. It’s just soft enough to get in my hair and oil the scalp, but it’s not greasy. Also, I need a healthy scalp. There’s a lot that’s happening to it every day. A lot of attention, especially as an actor, is on my hair and my scalp. It gets so much abuse trying to stay natural and also trying to be trendy. This is perfect.

entry.title: We Stopped 57 New Yorkers to Ask About Their Fall Shoes
entry.summary: Flats, loafers, and boots galore.
entry.content:
Now that temperatures have dipped in New York, open-toe season has come to a close. Sandals have swapped in for boots, loafers, and other cold-weather fare. Curious about what shoes New Yorkers are wearing this season, three Strategist writers canvassed the city, stopping people on street corners in the Flatiron District, Fort Greene, and the Upper East Side. We approached people on their way to the office, while they drank their afternoon coffees, as they were walking their dogs, and right before they hopped into an Uber with their groceries. We asked about comfortability and wearability, nodding knowingly when they gushed about the magic of zippers, blister-free leather, and the enduring appeal of Frye boots.

Ballet flats abounded in various heel heights, loafers showed up in different shapes and colors, and leathers, suedes, and croc-esque textures were on display. And as was the case when we asked New Yorkers about their work bags, plenty of secondhand and vintage finds sourced from eBay and Poshmark were in the mix, too. Below are all the shoes we spotted, shared with the permission — and thoughts — of their wearers.

“I’ve worn these Jeffrey Careful shoes for the past three months. They’re pretty much broken in; I wear them 24/7. I have a little bit of a bunion and they don’t bother me at all, or on the back of my ankle. They’re suede and leather and kind of like Tabis, which many of my friends have and need to resole. You can see the bottoms here — I’ve worn them a lot, and especially against New York City concrete sidewalks, the soles still look really good.”

“I got these in the Netherlands at the Posa store. I think they’re very cute — you can combine them with everything; that’s why I love them. And they’re very comfortable. I’ve had them for two months. I wear them to study, and yesterday, I walked 30,000 steps in them without any blisters or anything.”

“I love these because they are suede and very comfortable. I bought them about a year ago, actually. Straight out of the box, I wore them without any blisters. I walk a lot and wear these a lot, two to three miles at a time, and they still look pretty great.”

“The shoes are by a former ’70s Japanese brand called Haruta. I acquired them at Front General Store in Brooklyn. They’re super comfortable. I’ve owned them for about two years, but the wear on them does not reflect that.”

“I bought these in Park City, Utah. They’ve been interesting. It took me a little while to get used to them, but I like them now that I’ve broken them in. They feel sleek and cool.”

“I bought these on the RealReal. They took some breaking in and I had to add a thing in the back to make them more comfortable, but now I wear them all the time.”

“I wear them everywhere. Whenever I travel, I bring them because you can pair them with a casual fit but you can also dress them up.”

“I saw these in an ad and Google reverse-image searched. We were comparing them to Tabis last night. They’re Tabi-shaped but without the indentations.”

“I usually buy expensive shoes, but I took a chance on these. They’re from Zara, so I don’t know how long they’ll last. I got them in Paris.”

“I’ve had these for three months. They’re super comfortable. No break-in period. Daily 10,000 steps are no problem, and the most I’ve done in them is 25,000. I haven’t put on my Salomon sneakers in a very long time because of that. The cut in the front reminded me of the Loro Piana flat, which I wanted for so long. The rubber on these makes them really great for walking because I feel like they’re absorbing some of it. I love the little V in the front and the square toe. I think it’s, like, a really elegant shape.”

“I’ve had these for two seasons now. I also got them in tan suede. They come in a lot of different colors, and they’re really very comfortable for walking in the city. No blisters or breaking in — absolutely nothing. I think I may be getting them in burgundy. They’re so comfortable. Just put them on and go.”

“These are suede loafers from G.H.Bass, and I actually bought them recently. I was looking for something that looked nicer than a beat-up sneaker. They’re comfortable and I can slip them on easily when I’m walking my dog, Banchan.”

“I’m obsessed with them. It’s this French brand called Soeur. I wore them all summer long. I wear them almost every day. You can hike, you can run, you can dance, you can do anything — no issues. I want them to last forever.”

“I got them from the Korner. I’m from Hong Kong, and they’re a very popular Hong Kong brand. I love how versatile and comfortable they are. I wear them to conferences, work events, and also just on a nice Sunday afternoon. I’m usually in scrubs and Crocs, so it’s nice to wear something more cute.”

“I actually just got these yesterday from Asos. I work in a corporate office, so I’m trying to be professional but make it a little bit more fun.”

“They took a while to break it. I have another pair of Tony Bianco boots that were way more comfortable. These took maybe 15 times wearing them. I also went to town with a hair dryer. But now they are like slippers. Anytime where I used to wear a sneaker, now I wear these.”

“I was on the hunt for a long time for the perfect loafer. I saw these at a store in Easthampton and I was like, Okay, wait, these actually look exactly like the shoes that I want, because I wanted them to be comfortable and something that I can wear all the time. I’ve had them for a few months now, and they’ve stretched to my foot nicely because I’m walking everywhere. It’s been a perfect, comfortable everyday shoe. People think they’re The Row.”

“I’ve had these for years. They’re cute little pony-hair slingback flats from Schutz. They’re just so easy to slip on when I walk my dog. They look like slippers, right? But they have an elastic slingback. You’re the third person to compliment me on them. The thing is it’s a little bit of a conundrum sometimes because it has to be the exact right temperature. They’re sherpa-lined, so it can’t be too hot, but if it’s a little bit too chilly, like it was this morning, then I need to put socks on.”

“I was at a Buffalo Exchange in the Bay Area and saw these brown oiled Danskos and knew I had to add them to my Dansko collection. I have three pairs total: classic black, these brown, and a calf-leather kind of furry pair that people really love. I love the arch support. I love that you can kick them on and kick them off super easily. They’re heavy in the rotation. I will say the thing with Danskos is, for people who are not used to them, you have to figure out how to walk in them a little bit because of the platform. You have to be careful, or you will stumble. The city can be a little precarious for a Dansko wearer.”

“These are from a Japanese company called Hender Scheme, and they’re leather craftspeople. They normally make very simple, basic leather shoes, and then these were just a crazy mash-up that I thought were so exciting and had never seen before. This was my first purchase from the brand. I had been waiting for the diamond in the rough. They are incredible. Their craft and their quality as a maker in the shoe space really stands out.”

“These are Arc’teryx slide-on shoes. If you’re ever going climbing outside, they’re grippy for the mountain leading up to your climb. They’re also really comfortable and go with everything.”

“I’m wearing these amazing knee-high — I’d say white — boots from Frances Valentine. They’re literally so comfortable. They have a little block kitten heel. I have been wearing them for a few hours and could walk all around all day. I feel like the designer really knows what she’s doing. I mean, she knows that women in New York walk. I just got them for fall, like, a week ago. This is also the first time I’m wearing them, so this is the break-in walk, and I’m totally fine. I got them in red too. I’m very happy. They’re a good heel height too — not too high, not too short. Once it gets colder, I feel like it’ll look cute under pants also, so they’re really versatile.”

“These are my Steve Madden cowboy boots — but they have a zipper on the side, so they’re very easy to put on, not like a classic cowboy boot. I’ve had this shoe for, like, four years, and this is my second pair because they just wear in the heel a little bit. I loved them so much that I bought them again. They’re extremely comfortable. I walk very fast — like, I’m booking it getting on the subway — and I’m tall; I’m 5’9. So I feel like I’m naturally faster than people and step harder than people. So these wear well. I have to get another pair soon.”

“These are my party shoes. I’ve had them for over a year now, and they’re cute. I like that the fabric goes over the boot.”

“These are comfortable and easy to walk in. I also like that they zip on the side, so you don’t have to worry about the shoe strings.”

I just got these, they’re Sam Edelman. They’re brown leather and very cute.

“These are dupe Frye boots — like, 60 bucks on Amazon. We’ve been beep-bopping all day, no pain. Super comfy, would recommend!”

“I spent way too much money on these, but unfortunately, I love them. I wanted to hate them so I could return them and not feel guilty. I’m thankful for Afterpay.”

“I found these on Farfetch. I bought them on sale and still paid too much for them, but I love them so much. An Everywoman’s witchy October boot.”

“I bought them at Shoe Market on Bedford at the start of winter. I love the little square toe box, which is kind of fun, and I like that they’re actually quite comfortable. And they’re actually warm. I’m very much a form follows function kind of gal.”

“These were a Christmas gift I got about three years ago now. A great gift. One of my favorite pairs of shoes. They have a very nice wooden heel and definitely make a bit of a statement whenever I go out. The quality is kind of unmatched. They hold up. I’ve never had to take them to get fixed up at all. I take care of them; they take care of me.”

“One of my best friends works for the brand. She initially bought them in red, and I loved them so much, so she purchased them for me in black. I love how shiny they are, and I love the heel — it’s super chic but really easy to walk in. And I love how the toe is rounded. I’ve had them for about three or four years. They’re incredibly comfortable. I’ve probably walked 5,000 or 6,000 steps in these at a time. They just released an updated version with more of a pointy heel, and I did just purchase those as well.”

“I was looking for the perfect boot for two years. Knee-high, kitten heel, pointed toe. Took me so long to find them. I used to have a Naturalizer square-toe boot, and they stopped making that style. So I had to replace it, and I just decided to split up my needs: one pair that’s a cunty, pointy boot and one more heavy boot for everyday. So this is the pointy pair. They’re so comfortable. Naturalizer is a brand that’s known among older ladies for being super good on the feet. I wear them to work. I wear them to dinner. Any kind of event where I want to feel a little more fancy. But they are so comfortable that I could wear them dancing. Everyone should know about Naturalizer.”

“I actually got them on sale at Nordstrom, and they’re Nine West. They’re extremely comfortable. They’ve held up well while I commute. I easily walk two miles in them every day. They fit true to size on me, but I do have very narrow feet.”

“They’re black patent-leather Chelsea boots from J.Crew. They’re easy to slip on and walk around in. I was just on my way to the farmers’ market this morning, and it’s even easier than slipping on a pair of tennis shoes. The heel is starting to wear away a little bit, but this is after two solid seasons of use wearing them three to five days a week.”

“These are secondhand Danskos from Poshmark. I got them last week, and I’ve worn them almost every day. I love that they’re monochrome. I feel like it’s hard to find a heel that is also black when you’re looking for black boots. They’re supportive. And they just slip on. I only buy vegan leather usually, but now that I’m buying secondhand, I’m expanding into genuine leather, so now I’m going to get all the Danskos.”

“I got these two years ago. I saw some girl on TikTok had them, and I thought, I need those shoes, even though they’re more expensive than any shoes I’ve ever bought. They go with everything. They’re super cute. I’m short, so I always wear heels, but they kind of look like flats without being too much of a heel. They’re so comfortable. I walk 10,000 to 15,000 steps around the city. I was going to get them in another color, but I wear a half-size, and they stopped carrying 6.5.”

“A bit mainstream, but I thought they were a bit cute with the little heel. I’ve had them for two months, and they’re very comfortable.”

“I love these. Maison Margiela. They’re raffia, so I thought they’d be for the beach.”

“I picked them because I really like the color. I feel like it pops. And they’re comfortable.”

As most vintage shoes are no longer available, we included a few alternates for each pair.

“These are Golden Goose and I got them on the RealReal. I’ve had them for over a year now, and they’re very comfortable. I wear them a lot.”

“I have owned these for nine years and worn them across the country. I love them so much; they’re my best friends.”

“These are some worn-in brown boots from Frye that I stole from my boyfriend. I’ve had them for seven years. They’re leather that’s super worn in and soft. At this point, it’s like a second skin. I think that they’re pretty true to size. I do have a pretty bony foot, so thick socks are always a must for me — but with a thick sock, they do the job.”

“I thrifted these. Once it’s fall, I’m always excited to break my boots out. I was kind of rushing over here for work. So I said, What’s going to get me to and from while also maintaining some level of style? These are just always easy to wear. It’s nice to know that I can always come back to these. They’re classic.”

“I got these boots on eBay. I was looking for a new pair because the toe kept splitting on my favorite pair and I kept getting them repaired. So I just figured that I need to get real quality boots. The listing said they were handmade in Mexico. They are magic. I’ve walked 20 miles in Manhattan in them. They literally go with everything. I’m wearing them with a dress right now, but they look really cute with shorts. They also look really good under a pair of jeans, as well, with just the little toe poking out. My feet are a size 11, so every time I’m looking for shoes, especially on websites like eBay, I always just put my size in the search term because I’ll take whatever I can get. My guess is that they’re men’s boots because they are really wide.”
